title: Valid Parenthesis String with `*` wildcard — greedy min/max open-count range.
shortTitle: Valid Parenthesis String With `*` Wildcard — Greedy Min/Max Open-Count Range

s1_definition.profdef: This problem checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisk wildcards can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or an empty string. The greedy solution tracks a range of possible open-bracket counts, a low and a high, updating both as it scans, clamping the low at zero and rejecting if the high ever goes negative, and accepting if zero lies within the final range. It runs in linear time with constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has grouping strings where some markers are flexible placeholders that could act as an opener, a closer, or nothing. The validator keeps track of the smallest and largest number of still-open brackets that are possible so far. A flexible placeholder widens this range, a real opener raises both ends, and a real closer lowers both. If it is ever impossible to have any open brackets, even at the optimistic high end, the string fails; if at the end zero open brackets is achievable, it can be made valid.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track a low and high of possible open counts; clamp low at zero, fail if high goes negative, accept if zero is in range at the end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisk wildcards can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or an empty string. The greedy solution tracks a range of possible open-bracket counts, a low and a high, updating both as it scans, clamping the low at zero and rejecting if the high ever goes negative, and accepting if zero lies within the final range. It runs in linear time with constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has grouping strings where some markers are flexible placeholders that could act as an opener, a closer, or nothing. The validator keeps track of the smallest and largest number of still-open brackets that are possible so far. A flexible placeholder widens this range, a real opener raises both ends, and a real closer lowers both. If it is ever impossible to have any open brackets, even at the optimistic high end, the string fails; if at the end zero open brackets is achievable, it can be made valid.

**One line to remember:** Track a low and high of possible open counts; clamp low at zero, fail if high goes negative, accept if zero is in range at the end.

sections.s2_technical:
The asterisk makes a naive stack insufficient because each wildcard has three interpretations, and trying all combinations is exponential. The greedy insight is to track the range of possible counts of currently open brackets rather than a single count. You keep two numbers: low, the minimum possible open count, and high, the maximum possible open count, both starting at zero.

As you scan each character you update the range. For an opening bracket, both low and high increase by one, because it definitely adds an open bracket. For a closing bracket, both low and high decrease by one, because it definitely removes one. For an asterisk, the range widens: low decreases by one, since the asterisk could be a closing bracket reducing open count, and high increases by one, since it could be an opening bracket increasing it. The asterisk could also be empty, which is a value between, already covered by the range.

Two guards keep the range meaningful. If high ever becomes negative, it means even the most optimistic interpretation has more closers than openers at this point, which can never be valid, so you return false immediately. If low becomes negative, you clamp it to zero, because you can never have fewer than zero open brackets; a surplus of potential closers simply means some asterisks are treated as empty rather than as closers. Forgetting to clamp low would let it drift negative and wrongly reject valid strings.

A senior point is why checking low equals zero at the end is the acceptance test, not low at most zero. After clamping, low is the minimum achievable open count. The string can be made valid only if it is possible to end with exactly zero open brackets, and because high is at least low and the range is continuous, zero is achievable exactly when low has reached zero by the end. If low is still positive at the end, every interpretation leaves unmatched openers, so it fails.

Another senior point is that this greedy range method replaces a two-stack or dynamic-programming approach with constant space and a single pass, which is both simpler and faster. The alternative uses two stacks, one for opener indices and one for asterisk indices, matching greedily; it is correct but more code. For banking validation of flexible grouping strings the range method is my default.

A small finance-domain example: `int lo=0,hi=0; for(char c:s.toCharArray()){ if(c=='('){lo++;hi++;} else if(c==')'){lo--;hi--;} else {lo--;hi++;} if(hi<0) return false; if(lo<0) lo=0; } return lo==0;` validates a wildcard grouping string.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India accepts flexible grouping strings in a template system where an asterisk placeholder can stand for an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or nothing, and a validator must decide whether the template can be filled to form a balanced grouping. The templates are long, so validation must be linear. Checking a valid parenthesis string with wildcards is exactly this.

This is exactly how the wildcard validity check works in Java — tracking the range of possible open-bracket counts with a greedy low and high.

Problem 2 — A template may have more potential closers than openers at some point, which must fail only if even the optimistic interpretation is impossible, and leftover mandatory openers at the end must fail. This shows the high-goes-negative rejection, the low-clamp, and the end-low-equals-zero acceptance.

What the code will do: a `WildcardValidator` with `canBeValid(String template)` using the greedy min/max open-count range. The demo validates several wildcard templates.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the template `(*)`.

Step 1: low and high both start at zero. The first character is `(`, a real opener, so low becomes one and high becomes one. High is not negative and low is not negative, so no guard triggers.

Step 2: the next character is `*`, a wildcard. Low decreases by one to zero, since the asterisk could be a closer, and high increases by one to two, since it could be an opener. The range of possible open counts is now zero to two. Neither guard triggers.

Step 3: the next character is `)`, a real closer, so low decreases to minus one and high decreases to one. High is still non-negative. But low is now negative, so we clamp it to zero. The range is now zero to one.

Step 4: the scan ends. We check whether low equals zero, and it does, meaning it is possible to end with exactly zero open brackets, for example by treating the asterisk as empty so the string is just `()`. So the template can be made valid and we return true.

Step 5: for `(*))`, the extra closer is absorbed by treating the asterisk as an opener, and low still reaches zero at the end, so it is valid. For `)(`, the very first character is a closer, so low and high both go to minus one; high being negative triggers the immediate rejection, correctly identifying that no interpretation can fix a string starting with an unmatched closer.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO '(*)' CAN be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO '(*))' CAN be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO ')(' CANNOT be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "(*)"  low=0 high=0
    │ '(' low++,high++ ; ')' low--,high-- ; '*' low--,high++
    ▼
  '(' → low1 high1
  '*' → low0 high2
  ')' → low-1→clamp0  high1
    │ high<0 ever? no ; end low==0?
    ▼
  low==0 → true   (")(" → high<0 at i0 → false)
    ▼
  Output: can-be-valid yes/no
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Wildcard Validator ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Greedy interval tracking: [low, high] of open counts         │
  │  Guards: high<0 reject, clamp low>=0, end low==0 accept       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: validator only answers can-be-valid                       │
  │  O: swap to two-stack method without changing callers         │
  │  D: callers depend on the boolean result, not the range       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            WildcardValidator          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + canBeValid(template): boolean       │  O(n)/O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      canBeValid contract:
        Pre:  template non-null (else IllegalArgumentException)
        Post: true iff '*' can be filled to balance the string
        high<0 → false; clamp low to 0; accept iff low==0 at end

  ── State Diagram: Range Update ───────────────────────────

  [char] ──update low/high──→ [high<0? FALSE ; low<0? low=0]
      │ end
      ▼
  [low==0? true : false]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. WildcardValidatorDemo.main()
  2.   → canBeValid("(*)")
  3.     → track [low,high], guard high, clamp low
  4.     → end low==0
  5.     → return true
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parenthesis String with a wildcard checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisks can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opener, a closer, or empty. A naive stack fails because each wildcard has three interpretations, so instead of a single open count I track a range, a low and a high of the possible number of currently open brackets, in a single linear pass with constant space.

As I scan, an opener raises both low and high by one, a closer lowers both by one, and an asterisk widens the range, lowering low because it could be a closer and raising high because it could be an opener, with the empty interpretation covered in between. Two guards keep the range meaningful: if high ever goes negative, even the most optimistic interpretation has too many closers, so I reject immediately, and if low goes negative I clamp it to zero, because you can never have fewer than zero open brackets and extra potential closers just become empty asterisks.

The acceptance test is that low equals zero at the end. After clamping, low is the minimum achievable open count, and since the range is continuous up to high, ending with exactly zero open brackets is possible precisely when low has reached zero; if low is still positive, every interpretation leaves unmatched openers. I always explain why clamping low is essential, because without it the count drifts negative and wrongly rejects valid strings, which is the most common bug.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate flexible grouping templates where an asterisk placeholder can stand for an opener, a closer, or nothing, deciding whether a template can be filled to form a balanced grouping, in one linear pass. Explaining the low-high range, the three-way asterisk update, the high-negative rejection, the low-clamp, and the end-low-equals-zero acceptance shows the interviewer that I can reason about an ambiguous input with a clean greedy invariant instead of brute force.
